newsitem.title: USA: IMF gold sale plan still to be resolved.
newsitem.headline: IMF gold sale plan still to be resolved.

text.p: The future of a plan to sell a small portion of the International Monetary Fund's gold holdings to help relieve the debt of the world's poorest countries still hinges on the attitude of key wealthy nations, monetary sources said on Friday.
Although changes have been made to address the concerns of the poor nations and their supporters, the main hurdle facing the proposal is approval from wealthy donor countries.
Led by Germany, a number of European countries are opposed to the sale of IMF gold, arguing that the multilateral agency's responsibilities have grown so large that it needs to guard its gold.

IMF Managing Director Michel Camdessus has long favoured some small gold sales and has worked with the World Bank to develop a plan that would give relief to countries hopelessly weighed down by previous loans for the two agencies.

The multibillion-dollar initiative has already been debated without resolution at several meetings this year, including the leaders of the Group of Seven countries in France in June. It will come up for discussion again at the annual meeting of the IMF and World Bank that takes place Sept 25-Oct 3.
There is a precedent for selling IMF gold. Some was sold in the late 1970s to help developing countries hard hit by fast rising oil prices.

Under IMF rules, 85 percent of the total voting power of the agency's member countries is required before the precious metal can be sold, meaning that a relatively small number of countries could stand in the way.
The plan would help many countries in sub-Saharan Africa who face an impossible task in repaying loans made over the years to spur growth.

The IMF is also willing to consider the possibility of providing direct grants to countries, an idea that would have been almost unthinkable in the past since it smacks of debt forgiveness but this should please poorer countries.
In the IMF Survey newsletter of July 15, IMF director Jack Boorman, said a "possibility is to provide a grant to the country to help its obligations to the IMF."

The gold sales have also become part of a proposal by Camdessus to permanently finance the IMF's enhanced structual adjustment facility (ESAF). The gold sales would provide a pool of funds that would throw off income to provide assistance to the poor without going begging to developed countries every few years.
The IMF believes the ESAF programme might have to be terminated by early next century without new sources of assistance.
